```{r}
#| label: options

options(housepi.footer.sample = TRUE)
```

Bayesian data augmentation is a computational strategy that expands the parameter space by introducing latent variables (also referred to as hidden or augmented variables), so that a likelihood intractable on the observed data alone becomes tractable on the augmented data [@tanner_calculation_1987].

For example, consider a single infectious individual $i$.
Imagine that someone reported the date of symptom onset $T^\mathrm{ons}_{i}$.
We can think of the observation process that returned that value as some function of the true onset time, $t^\mathrm{ons}_{i}$.

We can introduce latent infection times $t_{i}$, defined as the difference between the onset time and the latent incubation period $\tau^\mathrm{inc}_{i}$, so that
$$t^\mathrm{ons}_{i} = t_{i} + \tau^\mathrm{inc}_{i},$$
where the incubation period is distributed according to a prior.

Let $x$ be the data of a single household (onset date and status), $z$ its latent variables (infection time and incubation period) and $\theta$ the vector of parameters.
The joint posterior then reads
$$p(\theta, z \mid x) \propto
  \underbrace{p^\mathrm{obs}(x \mid \theta, z)\, p^\mathrm{transm}(x \mid \theta, z)\, p^\mathrm{lat}(z \mid \theta)}_{\texttt{likelihood}}\;
  \underbrace{p(\theta)}_{\texttt{prior}},$$
where the reported `log_lik` gathers the transmission term $p^\mathrm{transm}$, the observation term $p^\mathrm{obs}$ and the latent-variable model $p^\mathrm{lat}$, while `lprior` is the parameter prior $p(\theta)$.
Without an observation node, $p^\mathrm{obs} = 1$.

The sections below define individual latent variables on minimal examples.

# Link arguments to source

Like parameters, latent variables need a model and a proposal for the MCMC sampler.
In many applications, latent variable definitions can also depend on the dataset or on model parameters to be inferred.

An argument value may name another definition of the model: a latent variable, a data column, an observation, a group rate or a parameter.
housepi looks the name up among the definitions the model carries, so each name must stand for one of them only^[A name nothing declares is an error, reported when the model is run, and so is a name two definitions claim.].
E.g. `visit_day` reads the individual data column "visit_day", `beta` the current value of the parameter "beta", while a number such as `14` is read as it is.

The convention applies to every definition argument, from `const`, `func`, `min` and `max` to the arguments of the model distribution, as in `model = "gamma", mean = mean, sd = sd`, reading the parameters "mean" and "sd".
Names combine into arithmetic expressions, such as `onset_date - incub_period` or `exposure_max + 0.99`, and can be passed to any of the functions listed by `browse_functions()`, e.g. `sqrt(beta)` or `min(onset_date)`.
An expression referencing no definition is instead evaluated once, when the definition is built: `max = 3 * 7` is stored as the plain value `21`, and a date such as `as.Date("2021-07-01")` collapses to its day count.

# Status specific definitions

In many applications, the same latent variable has to be augmented according to different rules depending on the individual.
Infection times of symptomatic and asymptomatic members are one example.
Status specific definitions apply to one status only, while generic definitions hold for every positive status.
Consider a survey that follows a household for 10 days from the first symptom onset, testing every member at the start and at the end of follow-up.
We tag symptomatic members with `status = 1` and asymptomatic ones with `status = 2`.
We augment infection times of symptomatic members as shown in [Get Started](housepi.html), informed by the reported onset date.
For asymptomatic members we sample the infection time within the follow-up period: transmission gives its probability, so it takes no `model`.

```{r}
#| label: status-specific-latent
#| warning: false
library(ggplot2)
library(housepi)
set_housepi_theme(colour_strips = TRUE)
set.seed(42)

onset_tommy <- 5
hh_model <- data.frame(id = c("tommy", "gina"),
                       hh_id = "house_1",
                       start_date = onset_tommy,
                       end_date = onset_tommy + 10,
                       status = c(1, 2),
                       onset_date = c(onset_tommy, NA)) |>
  new_housepi_model("case-ascertained") |>
  add_parameter(alpha = 0.001, beta = 0.07, gamma = 0.9, hh_size_ref = 4) |>
  add_infectivity_profile(import = "template") |>

  # associate latent definitions
  add_latent(
    # latent infection time for symptomatic members
    # here we use a generic definition
    infec_time = onset_date - incub_period,
    incub_period = list(model = "gamma", shape = 2, scale = 1),

    # latent infection time for asymptomatic members
    # here we use a status specific definition, with priority over generic
    infec_time = list(status = 2, min = start_date, max = end_date)
  )
```

To check how the latent draws evolve, pass the `id` of the individuals to follow to the argument `id_draws` of `run_inference()`.

```{r}
#| label: latent-infection-time-plot
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Density plots of latent infection times for two household members.
# run inference following traces of specific individuals
hh_model |>
  # store latent draws of "tommy" and "gina"
  run_inference(id_draws = c("tommy", "gina")) |>
  get_latent_draws("infec_time") |>
  bayesplot::mcmc_hist(facet_args = list(ncol = 1), alpha = 0.5, binwidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(data = data.frame(xintercept = onset_tommy),
             aes(xintercept = xintercept)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = onset_tommy + c(-10, 10))
```

Gina's infection time cannot precede the start of follow-up, Tommy's onset, and the model makes it more probable close to that bound.

# Example: estimate incubation period distribution

For simplicity, we start testing data augmentation on a dataset which is not a household survey.
Instead we consider a synthetic report documenting the days when a number of cases were exposed to infection and the days of symptom onset.
We simulate it with the "test" model (see `?template_test`), which carries no transmission dynamics, by chaining latent variables for each individual:

- the exposure window lasts 1 to 4 days, drawn from a categorical distribution (the draw is 0-based, so `exposure_days` counts the days after the first);
- the infection time `infec_time` is uniform within the exposure window;
- the incubation period `incub_period` is gamma distributed with the `mean` and `sd` we want to recover later;
- the onset time `onset_time` is their sum;
- `report_shift` marks a reporting error, which widens the onset interval by one day, earlier or later.

Observations with no `model` produce the reported columns: the last day of exposure and the first and last day of the reported onset interval.

```{r}
#| label: generate-delays-data
true_mean <- 2.2
true_sd <- 1.2
n_cases <- 223
dataset <- data.frame(id = seq_len(n_cases), hh_id = seq_len(n_cases),
                      status = 1) |>
  new_housepi_model("test") |>
  add_parameter(mean = !!true_mean, sd = !!true_sd) |>
  add_latent(
    exposure_days = list(model = "categorical",
                         d1 = 0.28, d2 = 0.34, d3 = 0.26, d4 = 0.12),
    infec_time = list(model = "uniform", max = exposure_days + 1),
    incub_period = list(model = "gamma", mean = mean, sd = sd),
    onset_time = infec_time + incub_period,
    report_shift = list(model = "categorical",
                        early = 0.135, exact = 0.73, late = 0.135)
  ) |>
  add_observation(
    exposure_max = exposure_days,
    onset_min = floor(onset_time) - max(1 - report_shift, 0),
    onset_max = floor(onset_time) + max(report_shift - 1, 0)
  ) |>
  run_simulation() |>
  # keep the reported columns only
  dplyr::select(id, hh_id, status, exposure_max, onset_min, onset_max)
head(dataset)
```
The data has no household structure, so every individual lives in a household of their own.

Assuming the incubation period to be described by a gamma distribution, we want to estimate its `mean` and `sd` by augmenting the infection and onset times.
Following the decomposition introduced above, the incubation period enters the *latent model* $p^\mathrm{lat}(z \mid \theta)$, while the reported onset day enters the *observation* term $p^\mathrm{obs}(x \mid \theta, z)$; both are reported in the pointwise `log_lik`.

For inference we keep the "test" model ($p^\mathrm{transm} = 1$) and build the whole augmentation from definitions:

- the infection time `infec_time` is drawn uniformly within the reported exposure window;
- the incubation period `incub_period` is the quantity we model, gamma distributed with the inferred `mean` and `sd` and bounded to a plausible range;
- the onset time `onset_time` follows deterministically as their sum.

Finally, an observation node ties the latent onset time to the data: we model the reported onset day `onset_mid` as a noisy measurement of the true onset time, normally distributed around `onset_time`.

```{r}
#| label: incubation-example-setup
# generate an instance of the household model class
hh_model <- dataset |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    # reported onset mid-point: noisy measurement of the reported interval
    onset_mid = 0.5 * (onset_min + onset_max + 1.)
  ) |>
  new_housepi_model("test") |>
  # define the gamma distribution parameters to be inferred
  add_parameter(
    mean = list(prior = "uniform", min = 0.1, max = 5),
    sd = list(prior = "uniform", min = 0.1, max = 5)
  ) |>
  # latent variable definitions
  add_latent(
    # infection time uniform within the reported exposure window
    # min = 0 by default for uniform; + 0.99 spans the whole reported day
    infec_time = list(model = "uniform", max = exposure_max + 0.99),
    # incubation period gamma by mean/std. deviation
    incub_period = list(model = "gamma", mean = mean, sd = sd,
                        min = 0.1, max = 14),
    # onset time follows deterministically as their sum
    onset_time = infec_time + incub_period
  ) |>
  # observation model for the observed mid-point
  add_observation("onset_mid", model = "normal", mean = onset_time, sd = 0.3)
```

```{r}
#| label: inference-traces
#| fig-height: 3
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Trace plots for mean and standard deviation parameters with three parallel chains.
#|  Overlaying orange lines indicate the values used for the simulation.
hh_fit <- hh_model |>
  # store latent draws of "7" and "13"
  run_inference(id_draws = c("7", "13"))

# plot traces of parameter draws
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(get_parameter_draws(hh_fit)) +
  geom_hline(data = data.frame(parameter = c("mean", "sd"),
                               simulated = c(true_mean, true_sd)),
             aes(yintercept = simulated))
```

```{r}
#| label: latent-draws-traces
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Trace plots for individual latent variables across three MCMC chains.
#|  Incubation period for two subjects (IDs 7 and 13).
# plot the traces of the incubation period alone
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(get_latent_draws(hh_fit, "incub_period"))
```

In this example we had to introduce the auxiliary latent variables `onset_time` and `infec_time`.
housepi samples every latent variable the likelihood reads, these two included, and stores a trace for each of them.
Passing `variable` to `get_latent_draws()` picks out the ones of interest.

A latent variable that no observation and no transmission term ever reads is a different case.
There is nothing to learn about it, so housepi does not sample it and it carries no trace.

# More about models and proposals

```{r}
#| label: color-scheme-latent
#| include: false
bayesplot::color_scheme_set(scheme = "orange")
```

Proposals for latent variables can be tried out on the "test" template, as in [Priors and proposals](priors_and_proposals.html).

A latent variable is sampled only where something reads it, so a playground needs an observation reading `z`.
A uniform observation over a window the variable can never leave contributes the same constant at every draw, which leaves the sampling to follow the model alone:

```{r}
#| label: latent inspection
#| warning: false

hh_fit <- data.frame(hh_id = 1, id = 1:2, status = 1, readout = 0) |>
  new_housepi_model(model = "test") |>
  add_latent("z", model = "normal", mean = 14) |>
  add_observation("readout", model = "uniform", loc = z,
                  min = -1e6, max = 1e6) |>
  run_inference()
```

```{r}
#| label: trace-latent-sample
#| fig-height: 2
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Trace plot of a single latent variable sampled from the model.
hh_fit |>
  get_latent_draws() |>
  bayesplot::mcmc_trace()
```

```{r}
#| label: trace-log-likelihood
#| fig-height: 2
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Trace plot of the pointwise per-household log-likelihood.
hh_fit |>
  get_log_lik_draws() |>
  bayesplot::mcmc_trace()
```
